comments.text: Starts tune A (0 to 3): stops all sound (sound_off), clears the three 35-byte voice blocks, copies the tune's speed from tune_table into the operand at $4173, gives each voice its order list from the table and the first pattern the list names, sets each voice's duration count to 1 so the next tick reads its first note, sets the transpose (the operand at $447E) to 0, clears the SID (sid_clear) and turns all three voices and the music on. One caller, $7D18, which always passes 0: tunes 1 to 3 are never started.

Voice 1's note flags, cleared at every new note. Bit 0 flips every frame; bit 1 marks a drum note (commands $83 and $8E), which plays noise on the frames bit 0 is set; bit 2 slide down ($84); bit 3 glide ($86 and $87), bit 7 its direction, up; bit 5 slide up ($85); bit 4 is set by an arpeggio byte and never tested. The block of 35 bytes from here is voice 1's state; voices 2 and 3 have the same layout at $40E6 and $4109, and the driver reaches each through X = 0, $23 or $46.
Voice 1, +1 and +2: the address of the next byte to read in the pattern, saved after each note.
Voice 1, +2: the high byte of the pattern pointer.
Voice 1, +3 and +4: the start of its order list (the list of pattern addresses the tune plays), where the list starts again after its closing zero word.
Voice 1, +4: the order list's high byte.
Voice 1, +5 and +6: the offset in the order list of the next pattern address, in bytes; 2 after a tune starts, since the first entry is read at once.
Voice 1, +6: the order offset's high byte.
Voice 1, +7 and +8: how far a slide has moved the frequency so far; it grows by the slide step every frame, so the pitch moves at a rate that keeps rising. Cleared by the slide commands.
Voice 1, +8: the slide total's high byte.
Voice 1, +9 and +10: the arpeggio table in use, set by a byte $C0-$CF from arp_ptr_lo/hi; arpeggio 0 is a single 0, a note played straight.
Voice 1, +10: the arpeggio pointer's high byte.
Voice 1, +11: the position in the arpeggio table, moved on every frame and set back to 0 after an entry with bit 7 set.
Voice 1, +12 and +13: the slide step, added to the slide total every frame once the delay has run out.
Voice 1, +13: the slide step's high byte.
Voice 1, +14: frames before a slide starts; counted down, then held at 1 so the slide runs every frame after.
Voice 1, +15: ticks left of the current note; at 0 the next pattern bytes are read.
Voice 1, +16: the note length in ticks set by the last byte $E0-$FF (1 to 32), given to every note after it.
Voice 1, +17: the note number, 0 for C1, in semitones; a glide moves it one step a tick.
Voice 1, +18: attack and decay for the SID, set by a byte $D0-$DF with the release byte after it, and cleared by a rest.
Voice 1, +19: sustain and release for the SID.
Voice 1, +20 and +21: the frequency worked out this frame (note, arpeggio, transpose, vibrato, slide and drum), which mus_play writes to the SID.
Voice 1, +21: the frequency's high byte.
Voice 1, +22 and +23: the pulse width, set by command $8F and moved by the pulse sweep.
Voice 1, +23: the pulse width's high byte, the one the sweep's limits are compared with.
Voice 1, +24: 1 when a note has just been read, so mus_play writes the waveform once without its gate bit and then with it, to start the envelope again; a rest clears it.
Voice 1, +25: the vibrato's depth; the position swings between 0 and twice this, and the offset is the position less the depth.
Voice 1, +26: how far the vibrato position moves each frame.
Voice 1, +27: the vibrato position.
Voice 1, +28: bit 6 vibrato on (commands $81 and $82), bit 5 the position is falling. Bit 7 would move the vibrato only on alternate frames, but nothing sets it.
Voice 1, +29: the pulse sweep's lower limit, a high byte of pulse width (command $90).
Voice 1, +30: the pulse sweep's upper limit.
Voice 1, +31: added to or taken from the pulse width every frame by the sweep.
Voice 1, +32: 0 no sweep, 1 the pulse width rising, $81 falling; it turns at each limit.
Voice 1, +33: the waveform chosen by the pattern ($10 triangle, $20 sawtooth, $40 pulse, $80 noise, $14 triangle with ring modulation, $12 triangle with sync), without the gate bit.
Voice 1, +34: the waveform for this frame: the voice's own, or noise on a drum note's alternate frames.
Voice 2's 35-byte block, laid out as voice 1's at $40C3; this is its flags byte. The start of a tune clears it and fills in its order list and pattern pointer.
Voice 2's pattern pointer, low byte (+1), set when a tune starts.
Voice 2's pattern pointer, high byte (+2).
Voice 2's order list address, low byte (+3).
Voice 2's order list address, high byte (+4).
Voice 2's order offset (+5), and the rest of its block up to the duration count, reached only through X = $23.
Voice 2's duration count (+15), set to 1 when a tune starts.
Voice 2's attack and decay (+18), which mus_play writes to $D40C.
Voice 2's sustain and release (+19), written to $D40D.
Voice 2's frequency for this frame, low byte (+20), written to $D407.
Voice 2's frequency for this frame, high byte (+21), written to $D408.
Voice 2's pulse width, low byte (+22), written to $D409.
Voice 2's pulse width, high byte (+23), written to $D40A.
Voice 2's new-note flag (+24), and the vibrato bytes after it.
Voice 2's vibrato flags (+28), cleared when a tune starts, and its sweep limits and step.
Voice 2's pulse sweep state (+32), cleared when a tune starts, and its waveform (+33).
Voice 2's waveform for this frame (+34), written to $D40B.
Voice 3's 35-byte block, laid out as voice 1's at $40C3; this is its flags byte.
Voice 3's pattern pointer, low byte (+1).
Voice 3's pattern pointer, high byte (+2).
Voice 3's order list address, low byte (+3).
Voice 3's order list address, high byte (+4).
Voice 3's order offset (+5), and the rest of its block up to the duration count.
Voice 3's duration count (+15), set to 1 when a tune starts.
Voice 3's attack and decay (+18), written to $D413.
Voice 3's sustain and release (+19), written to $D414.
Voice 3's frequency for this frame, low byte (+20), written to $D40E.
Voice 3's frequency for this frame, high byte (+21), written to $D40F.
Voice 3's pulse width, low byte (+22), written to $D410.
Voice 3's pulse width, high byte (+23), written to $D411.
Voice 3's new-note flag (+24), and the vibrato bytes after it.
Voice 3's vibrato flags (+28), cleared when a tune starts, and its sweep limits and step.
Voice 3's pulse sweep state (+32), cleared when a tune starts, and its waveform (+33).
Voice 3's waveform for this frame (+34), written to $D412.
Calls of mus_play left before the next tick, when every voice steps through its pattern; reloaded from the tune's speed (the operand at $4173).
Counts calls of sound_irq down from 10; the tenth call plays nothing, so the music and the effects run on 9 interrupts in 10.
Non-zero while a tune plays; set by mus_start_tune, cleared by sound_off and so by command $91.
Non-zero when mus_play may write voice 1 to the SID; the sound effect routines take voices 1 and 3 and the alarm takes voice 2 while they sound, but nothing calls them, so all three stay on.
Non-zero when mus_play may write voice 2 to the SID; cleared and set again only by the alarm, which nothing calls.
Non-zero when mus_play may write voice 3 to the SID.
Non-zero while a sound effect plays (sfx_start); nothing calls sfx_start, so it stays 0.
Non-zero while the alarm sounds on voice 2 (alarm_start); nothing calls alarm_start, so it stays 0.
The alarm's period, the value alarm_start was given: 0 continuous noise, 7 a steady tone, any other value a tone broken by noise every period plus one ticks.
Counts the alarm's period down.
Scratch for mus_voice_sound: twice the vibrato depth, the top of the position's swing.
Scratch for mus_voice_sound: the vibrato offset, scaled by the note's octave, added to the frequency.
Scratch for mus_voice_sound: the vibrato offset's high byte, $FF when it is below zero.
The master volume written to $D418 every time mus_play runs; sid_clear sets it to 15 and nothing else writes it.

The sound's part of the raster interrupt, called from $6264: saves the pointer at $F0, then on nine calls in ten plays the music (mus_play) and the sound effects (sfx_play); the tenth only reloads the counter sound_skip.

One call of the music: returns at once unless mus_on. Counts mus_tick down and at 0 steps each voice through its pattern (mus_voice_step) and reloads the count from the tune's speed. Then works out each voice's sound for this frame (mus_voice_sound) and writes frequency, pulse width, envelope and waveform for each voice whose enable byte is set, giving the waveform once without its gate bit first when a new note starts, and finally the volume.

The operand of `lda #$06` here is the tune's speed, the calls of mus_play between ticks, written by mus_start_tune from the tune's entry: 6, 8, 8 and 5 for tunes 0 to 3. The code from here reloads the tick count, gets each voice's sound and writes the SID.

The pattern commands $80 to $95, one handler address each, read by mus_voice_step into the jump at $4454: $80 rest, $81 vibrato off, $82 on, $83 drum, $84 slide down, $85 slide up, $86 glide down, $87 glide up, $88 end of pattern, $89 vibrato setting, $8A noise, $8B pulse, $8C sawtooth, $8D triangle, $8E drum, $8F pulse width, $90 pulse sweep, $91 stop the music, $92 triangle with ring modulation, $93 triangle with sync, $94 transpose, $95 tie. A byte $96-$BF would take its address from the code after the table.
The high bytes of mus_commands, read one byte on from the low bytes with the same index ($444E).

Commands $80 (rest) and, from $4275, $95 (tie). A rest clears the new-note flag and the voice's envelope, so the note just played falls silent, and the voice waits one note length; a tie only waits, so the note before it goes on sounding.
Command $95, the tie: the voice waits another note length without a new note, so the note before goes on sounding (it shares the end of cmd_rest).

Command $94: the next pattern byte becomes the transpose, the operand at $447E, added to every note of every voice from then on. Only tune 0's third voice uses it, to shift the whole tune down a tone ($FE) and back.
Command $90: three bytes, the lower and upper limits of the pulse width's high byte and the step added each frame; starts the sweep rising.
Commands $8A to $8D and $92, $93: each sets the voice's waveform ($80 noise, $40 pulse, $20 sawtooth, $10 triangle, $14 triangle with ring modulation, $12 triangle with sync).
Command $8B: the voice's waveform becomes pulse ($40).
Command $8C: the voice's waveform becomes sawtooth ($20).
Command $8D: the voice's waveform becomes triangle ($10).
Command $92: the voice's waveform becomes triangle with ring modulation ($14).
Command $93: the voice's waveform becomes triangle with sync ($12).
Command $8F: the next byte is the pulse width's high byte; the low byte is cleared and the sweep stopped.

Command $91: drops the return into mus_play and goes to sound_off, which stops the music and silences the SID; the voices after this one are not stepped this tick. Tunes 1 to 3 end with it in voice 1, which is why their other voices need no end.
Command $88: the voice moves to the next pattern in its order list; at the zero word that ends the list it goes back to the first, so a tune that ends its patterns with $88 plays for ever.

Commands $85 (slide up, from here) and $84 (slide down, from $4335): three bytes, the slide step (two) and the frames before it starts; the slide total is cleared. The slide lasts until the next note clears the flags.
Command $84, slide down: sets flag bit 2 and reads the same three bytes as the slide up, step and delay; the code after the flag is shared by both and also clears the slide total.
Command $89: two bytes, the vibrato's step and its depth; the position starts at the depth, the middle of its swing. Command $82 turns the vibrato on.

Commands $87 (glide up, from here) and $86 (glide down, from $4389): the note number moves a semitone each tick until the next note. Command $86 goes wrong: it stores the accumulator, which holds $43, the high byte of its own address, with bit 3 added, so the flags become $4B and the voice also plays as a drum. No tune uses $86 or $87.

Command $86, glide down. The `ldy` here was surely meant to be `lda`: as it is, the accumulator still holds $43 from the jump, and the flags become $4B instead of the old flags with bit 3 added. The glide does run downward, but bits 0 and 1 make the note a drum as well. No tune uses $86.
Command $81: vibrato off.
Command $82: vibrato on.
Commands $83 and $8E: the note is a drum, alternating frame by frame between its waveform and noise pitched high above it. No tune uses them.

One tick of the voice at X ($00, $23 or $46): counts its duration down; while the note lasts it only moves a glide. At 0 it clears the flags and reads pattern bytes until a note: $00-$7F a note (0 is C1), which starts with the new-note flag and lasts the current length; $80-$BF a command through mus_commands; $C0-$CF an arpeggio table; $D0-$DF an envelope, attack/decay and sustain/release in the next two bytes; $E0-$FF the length of the notes that follow, 1 to 32 ticks. Saves the pointer after the note.
The operand of this `jmp` is written just before it with the command's handler from mus_commands; the handlers go back to the read loop at $43BF.
The low byte of the jump's operand, written at $444B with the handler's low byte.
The high byte of the jump's operand, written at $4451; the jump goes to the handler, and every handler ends by going back to $43BF.

Works out the voice at X for this frame: the note plus the arpeggio table's next entry plus the transpose (the operand at $447E) gives the frequency from freq_table; then the vibrato swing, the slide, the pulse sweep and a drum's noise frames are applied, and the frequency and waveform left for mus_play to write. The vibrato offset is doubled once for every 24 semitones the note is below note 96, so lower notes get the larger offset.

The operand of `adc #$00` here is the transpose, in semitones, written by command $94 and set to 0 when a tune starts; it applies to all three voices. The code from here looks up the frequency, swings the vibrato, moves the slide and the sweep, and picks the waveform.
Twelve frequencies for the octave below C1, C0 to B0 (C0 = $0116), which no note reaches: the lookup starts at freq_table, note 0.
The SID frequency for each note, 83 words from C1 ($022C) to A#7 ($F880), each octave double the one before, for the PAL clock; the note number indexes it by words.
The second byte onward of freq_table, read with the same index as its low bytes ($4487); the 83 words run to $4695.
The low bytes of the 16 arpeggio tables' addresses, for pattern bytes $C0 to $CF.
The high bytes of the 16 arpeggio tables' addresses; all $46.

Sixteen arpeggio tables, semitones added to the note on successive frames, the last of each with bit 7 set to start again: 0 the note alone; 1 a minor chord (0, 3, 7); 2 major (0, 4, 7); 3 (0, 2, 7); 4 (0, 4, 7, 12); 5 (7, 12, 15); 6 (7, 12, 16); 7 (3, 7, 12); 8 (4, 7, 12); 9 (0, 12); 10 (0, 3, 10); 11 (0, 5, 7); 12 (5, 0); 13 (0, 7); 14 four frames of the note and one an octave up; 15 (2, 0). The tunes use 0, 1, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 14.

The four tunes, seven bytes each: the speed (calls of mus_play to a tick), then the order lists of voices 1, 2 and 3. Tune 0 (speed 6) is the title and game music; tunes 1 and 2 (speed 8) and 3 (speed 5) are jingles a few seconds long, which nothing starts.
Tune 0's entry in tune_table, from its second byte: the order lists of voices 1 ($46FF), 2 ($476D) and 3 ($477F), low byte first, read at $4028 to $4068 with X = 0 for tune 0, 7 for tune 1 and so on.
The high byte of a tune's voice 1 order list (tune_table +2).
The low byte of a tune's voice 2 order list (tune_table +3).
The high byte of a tune's voice 2 order list (tune_table +4).
The low byte of a tune's voice 3 order list (tune_table +5).

The high byte of a tune's voice 3 order list (tune_table +6), and from $46EA the entries of tunes 1 to 3: speed 8 with lists at $4943, $4947 and $494B; speed 8 with $498E, $4992, $4996; speed 5 with $49D7, $49DB, $49DF.

Tune 0, voice 1's order list, 54 pattern addresses and a closing zero word: the intro (t0_v1_intro), the bass riff t0_v1_riff_c five times, then six rounds of the bass line in C, F and G (t0_v1_bass_c, _f, _g), after which the list starts again. 1,040 ticks in all, the same as the other two voices, so the three start again together.
Tune 0, voice 2's order list: its intro, its bridge, then its chord pattern six times, 1,040 ticks, and a closing zero word.

Tune 0, voice 3's order list: its intro, the bridge twice, the two halves of the melody, the transpose down a tone, the melody's first half again and the transpose back, 1,040 ticks, and a closing zero word.
Tune 0, voice 1, the intro (192 ticks): triangle with a wide vibrato, six notes from C6 to D#6, then pulse with a sweeping width for a slow bass of G2 and C2, 32 ticks each.

Tune 0, voice 1, the riff on C (16 ticks): sets a new envelope and sweep, then pulse C2 notes two ticks apart with a high triangle-and-ring-modulation blip (A#7, A#6) between them; it ends by setting the envelope and vibrato the following bass patterns keep.
Tune 0, voice 1, the bass on C (16 ticks): the same pulse C2 pattern as the riff, with its ring-modulated blips, without the settings.
Tune 0, voice 1, the bass on F (16 ticks): F1 and F2 on pulse with the ring-modulated blips.
Tune 0, voice 1, the bass on G (16 ticks): G1 and G2 on pulse with the ring-modulated blips.
Tune 0, voice 2, the intro (192 ticks): a short rest, then triangle with vibrato from G5 to D#6, answering voice 1, then pulse chords on arpeggio 1 (minor) at G5 and C5.
Tune 0, voice 2, the bridge (80 ticks): minor-chord arpeggios on G5 and C5, 20 ticks each.
Tune 0, voice 2, the chords under the melody (128 ticks): arpeggio chords on C5, F4, G4 and C4, 32 ticks each, played six times.
Tune 0, voice 3, the intro (192 ticks): triangle, then a fast pulse figure on D#6, G5, A#5 and D6 or C6, and the same figure in single ticks across two octaves.
Tune 0, voice 3, the bridge (40 ticks), played twice: a vibrato figure on arpeggio 14 (an octave blip every fifth frame), D#5 to C5 and the same an octave up.
Tune 0, voice 3, the first half of the melody (256 ticks): long notes from C4 to D#5 with vibrato and two pitch slides down that tie into the next note.
Tune 0, voice 3, the second half of the melody (256 ticks): a figure around G5 repeated four times, with slides down to C5 and up to B5 and a last long slide down from C6.
Tune 1's three order lists, one pattern each, every one closed by a zero word: voice 1 t1_v1, voice 2 t1_v2, voice 3 t1_v3. Nothing starts tune 1.
Tune 1, voice 1: C3 then G2 on pulse, 20 ticks, then $91, which stops the music. A two-note jingle nothing plays.
Tune 1, voice 2: sawtooth chords on C5 and G4 for the jingle's 20 ticks; the bytes after them would run into voice 3's pattern and on into tune 2's order lists, but voice 1 stops the tune first.
Tune 1, voice 3: a pulse figure G5, F#5, E5 and B4, 20 ticks; what follows its last note is never read.
Tune 2's three order lists, one pattern each, closed by zero words. Nothing starts tune 2.
Tune 2, voice 1: a low C#2 on pulse for 24 ticks, then $91, which stops the music.
Tune 2, voice 2: G#4, D#5 and a long G5 with vibrato, 24 ticks; the rest is never read.
Tune 2, voice 3: a rest, C#5 and a long G#5 with vibrato, 24 ticks; the rest is never read.
Tune 3's three order lists, one pattern each, closed by zero words. Nothing starts tune 3.
Tune 3, voice 1: a pulse bass C2, D#2, F2, G#2 and a long G2, 48 ticks, then $91, which stops the music.
Tune 3, voice 2: the same rising figure on G3 to D#4 and a long C3, 48 ticks; the rest is never read.
Tune 3, voice 3: the figure on C4 to G#4 with an octave-blip arpeggio and a long C4 chord, 48 ticks; it runs on into tune 0's t0_v3_tone_up, which is never reached from here.
Tune 0, voice 3: sets the transpose back to 0 and ends the pattern, after the melody's second playing.
Tune 0, voice 3: sets the transpose to -2, so all three voices play a tone lower for the next 256 ticks, and ends the pattern.

Starts an alarm on voice 2 with period A (see alarm_period): takes the voice from the music, sets a high frequency ($64xx), no attack or decay and sustain 6, starts noise when the period is 0 and triangle otherwise, sets the volume to 15 and turns the alarm on; alarm_tick then keeps it going. Nothing calls it: no instruction names it and no pointer in the image holds its address.
Stops the alarm: clears its flag and voice 2's envelope and gives voice 2 back to the music. Nothing calls it.

Starts sound effect A (0 to 16): takes voices 1 and 3 from the music, copies the effect's 20-byte record from sfx_table into sfx_state through the operand at $4AAA, which this rewrites, and sets the two voices' frequencies, attack and decay, pulse widths and waveforms, gating each; sets the volume to 15 and sfx_on. Nothing calls it: no instruction names it and no pointer in the image holds its address.
The low byte of the copy's source address, written by sfx_start from sfx_table; it holds $EC, the assembler's value, since nothing has called sfx_start.
The high byte of the copy's source, written from sfx_table +1. The code after the copy loads both voices from the record and starts them.
The addresses of the 17 sound effects' records, sfx_0 to sfx_16, read only by sfx_start.
The high bytes in sfx_table, read with the same index as the low bytes ($4AA1).
Sound effect 0, never played: 36 steps; voice 1 pulse from $040A, rising by $0200 a step; voice 3 pulse from $0328, rising by $0300 a step; back to the start every 18 steps, 2 times.
Sound effect 1, never played: 20 steps; voice 1 triangle with ring modulation from $1E33, rising by $0A01 a step; voice 3 noise from $1433, falling by $0400 a step.
Sound effect 2, never played: 20 steps; voice 1 pulse from $0C00, falling by $0200 a step; voice 3 noise from $1300, falling by $0200 a step; back to the start every 6 steps, 5 times.
Sound effect 3, never played: 25 steps; voice 1 noise from $0800, rising by $00FA a step; voice 3 noise from $1364, rising by $01FA a step.
Sound effect 4, never played: 50 steps; voice 1 triangle with ring modulation from $0C34, falling by $0A01 a step; voice 3 noise from $2334, falling by $0E07 a step.

Sound effect 5, never played: 200 steps; voice 1 noise from $0101, steady; voice 3 pulse from $0265, rising by $0196 a step; back to the start every 6 steps, 99 times; voice 1 shifted by the random number at each restart.
Sound effect 6, never played: 40 steps; voice 1 triangle from $2F00, falling by $0028 a step; voice 3 triangle from $3100, falling by $0028 a step; back to the start every 5 steps, 6 times.
Sound effect 7, never played: 40 steps; voice 1 triangle from $1B00, falling by $0028 a step; voice 3 triangle from $1550, falling by $0028 a step; back to the start every 5 steps, 6 times.

Sound effect 8, never played: 20 steps; voice 1 triangle with ring modulation from $0400, rising by $0114 a step; voice 3 noise from $1D00, falling by $0464 a step; back to the start every 6 steps, 4 times; voice 1 shifted by the random number at each restart.

Sound effect 9, never played: 15 steps; voice 1 noise from $0E00, falling by $0300 a step; voice 3 noise from $0D00, falling by $0100 a step; back to the start every 12 steps, 5 times; voice 1 shifted by the random number at each restart.
Sound effect 10, never played: 25 steps; voice 1 noise from $3000, falling by $0005 a step; voice 3 noise from $1364, rising by $0005 a step; back to the start every 10 steps, 99 times.
Sound effect 11, never played: 20 steps; voice 1 pulse from $1D00, falling by $0200 a step; voice 3 noise from $2A50, falling by $0300 a step; back to the start every 13 steps, 6 times.
Sound effect 12, never played: 15 steps; voice 1 noise from $2A00, rising by $0300 a step; voice 3 noise from $3100, rising by $0300 a step.
Sound effect 13, never played: 10 steps; voice 1 pulse from $3100, rising by $0128 a step; voice 3 pulse from $2B00, rising by $0128 a step; back to the start every 5 steps, 6 times.

Sound effect 14, never played: 20 steps; voice 1 triangle with ring modulation from $3C00, falling by $0032 a step; voice 3 triangle with ring modulation from $4500, falling by $0032 a step; back to the start every 5 steps, 6 times.

Sound effect 15, never played: 20 steps; voice 1 triangle with ring modulation from $3900, falling by $003C a step; voice 3 triangle with ring modulation from $4F00, falling by $003C a step; back to the start every 5 steps, 6 times.
Sound effect 16, never played: 5 steps; voice 1 pulse from $2880, falling by $0046 a step; voice 3 pulse from $5000, falling by $0046 a step; back to the start every 2 steps, 6 times.
Ends a sound effect: clears sfx_on and the envelopes of voices 1 and 3 and gives them back to the music; then, as at $4CA3, one tick of the alarm (alarm_tick).

One tick of the alarm, while alarm_on: voice 2 holds triangle, with a frame of noise each time the period runs out, unless the period is 7, which never breaks the tone. Writes only voice 2's control register.

One tick of the sound effects, from sound_irq: first moves the random number on (random); then, while sfx_on, counts the effect's duration down, ending it at 0 (sfx_end). An effect advances one step a call, nine frames in ten. Each time the repeat timer runs out and repeats are left it puts both voices back on their starting frequencies, voice 1's high byte plus the random number when the record asks; between times it slides each voice up or down by its step; once the repeats are spent the pitches hold until the steps run out. Then the alarm's tick.

The sound effect in play: its 20-byte record as sfx_start copied it ($4D98 the steps left), then the working repeat timer ($4DAC) and the two voices' frequencies ($4DAD voice 1, $4DAF voice 3). Each record holds: steps; repeat period; voice 1's and voice 3's frequencies; their attack/decay; their waveforms; their pulse widths' high bytes; voice 1's and voice 3's slide steps; the slide directions (1 up, $FF down, 0 none); the number of repeats; and a flag that adds the random number to voice 1's pitch at each repeat.
The effect's repeat period in steps (+1).
Voice 1's starting frequency, low byte (+2).
Voice 1's starting frequency, high byte (+3).
Voice 3's starting frequency, low byte (+4).
Voice 3's starting frequency, high byte (+5).
Voice 1's attack and decay (+6), written to $D405.
Voice 3's attack and decay (+7), written to $D413.
Voice 1's waveform (+8), written to $D404 without and then with the gate bit.
Voice 3's waveform (+9), written to $D412 the same way.
Voice 1's pulse width, high byte (+10), written to $D403.
Voice 3's pulse width, high byte (+11), written to $D411.
Voice 1's slide step, low byte (+12); the step is 16 bits, +12 and +13.
Voice 1's slide step, high byte (+13).
Voice 3's slide step, low byte (+14); +14 and +15.
Voice 3's slide step, high byte (+15).
Voice 1's slide direction (+16): 1 up, $FF (any value with bit 7) down, 0 none.
Voice 3's slide direction (+17).
Repeats left (+18): how many more times the voices go back to their starting pitches.
The random flag (+19): non-zero adds the random number to voice 1's frequency high byte at each repeat.
The repeat timer, reloaded from sfx_period.
Voice 1's current frequency, low byte, then high byte at $4DAE.
Voice 1's current frequency, high byte.
Voice 3's current frequency, low byte, then high byte at $4DB0.
Voice 3's current frequency, high byte.
Stops the music, the sound effect and the alarm (their flags to 0) and goes on into sid_clear. Called by mus_start_tune and by command $91.
Writes 0 to the SID's 24 registers $D400-$D417 and 15 to the volume, both at $D418 and in mus_volume.

Moves the 32-bit shift register at random_seed on by one bit and returns its first byte in A. The bit shifted in comes from bits 3 and 6 of that byte, added to $38 so that it carries out of bit 7; sfx_play calls it on every tick it gets, so it runs whether or not an effect plays. Only the unused effects read it.
The random number's 32-bit shift register, four bytes, the first the one returned; $FF $80 $1B $34 when the game starts.
The shift register's second byte; its top bit moves into random_seed at each step.
The shift register's third byte.
The shift register's last byte, which takes in the new bit.
Two bytes before the big digits ($EA $00) that the digit drawing never reads: it starts at '0', at $4DEE.

Ten digits, '0' to '9', 16 bytes each, a byte a row of 8 pixels, in the style of a seven-segment display: two empty rows, the top bar, five rows of upright strokes, the middle bar, five rows more, the bottom bar and an empty row. The routine at $7906 finds digit d at $4DEE + 16 × d. Digit 9 ends at $4E8D, where the game's variables after it begin.
When bit 7 is set, the interrupt does not count delay_count down; nothing writes it, so it stays 0.
The raster line of the interrupt, set to $EB at start-up and written back to $D012 by each interrupt.
When non-zero, the interrupt does not count delay_count down; nothing writes it, so it stays 0.
Scratch for most_liked and least_liked ($946B, $94C2): the country found so far, $FF for none.
Scratch for the census at $BE64: how many countries pass each test.
Three bytes nothing reads, $4C $10 $08: the instruction `jmp $0810`, left from an earlier start-up.

Where the loader hands over (`jmp $4E96` from $03F3, with $01 = $14). Seeds the random number generator (random_init, $7BFF), sets up a new game (new_game, $924C), sets $5B51 and $5B52 to 1, copies the 801 bytes of state at $5B50 to the RAM save at $1000 (copy_block), so that RAMLOAD before any RAMSAVE gives back the start, and goes on to cold_start ($7C52).
copy_block's six inline bytes: from $5B50 to $1000, $21 bytes and 3 pages ($0321 in all).
After the copy, on to the game's cold start at $7C52, which never returns here.
Four zero bytes between the start-up and the script engine's handler table that nothing reads.
One bit set in each byte, bit 0 to bit 7 ($01 to $80): turns a sprite number into its bit for $D015 and $D010, and the joystick reader tests bits of its byte against the first five.
bit_masks for bit 1 ($02), the joystick's down bit, named by the test at $513A.
bit_masks for bit 2 ($04), the joystick's left bit, named at $5140.
bit_masks for bit 3 ($08), the joystick's right bit, named at $5146.
bit_masks for bit 4 ($10), the fire bit, named at $514D; the last three masks, $20 to $80, follow.
Each byte with one bit clear, bit 0 to bit 7 ($FE to $7F): selects one keyboard column for the key test (key_down) and clears a sprite's bit in $D015.

Tables of a graphics library that nothing in the game reads: left-edge masks $00 to $FE, right-edge masks $FF to $01, a $00 and $FF, single bits $80 to $01, single gaps $7F to $FE, and at $4F7F the multiples of 8 from 0 to 248.

The bitmap address of each character row of the game's picture, 26 words: row r at $E160 + r × 320, so row 0 is the C64's second row and every row starts 4 cells in, the 256 by 192 pixel area of the Spectrum original centred in the C64's 320 by 200. Only rows 0 to 23 are used; the last two words are $FF60 and $E020.
bitmap_rows from its first high byte, read with the same index ($7218, $731C).

The address in screen memory (the colour cells, $DC00) of each character row, 26 words: row r at $DC2C + r × 40, the same 32 by 24 area as bitmap_rows. Rows 24 and 25 ($DFEC and $DC04) are never asked for.
screen_rows from its first high byte, read with the same index.
A becomes its absolute value. From here to $50AC is a library of arithmetic nothing in the game calls: no instruction names these addresses.
The integer square root of the 16-bit number at $36: subtracts the odd numbers 1, 3, 5 and so on until it goes below zero, leaving the count in $3D. Never called.
The square of A's absolute value into $36/$37, by unused_multiply. Never called.
$33 times $35, eight bits by eight, into $36/$37, keeping X. Never called.
The same multiplication as unused_multiply without saving X. Never called.
The 16-bit number in X (low) and Y (high) divided by A: the quotient in $7A/$7B, the remainder in $7C. Never called.
Divides the 16-bit number at $76/$77 by the one at $74/$75: the quotient in $76/$77, the remainder in $78/$79, one bit at a time. One caller, $BA1A.
Y becomes A times 6. Never called.
Reads the controls (read_controls) and returns the directions and fire just pressed, those set now and not on the last call, keeping the last reading in $55. Never called.
Is the key whose matrix position is in X down? The high nibble of X is the keyboard column, the low nibble the row; returns with the carry set when it is. Banks the I/O in and out around the test.
Takes the next nibble of $04 (high first) and returns its column or row select byte from clear_masks.

Reads the player's control through the routine named at $512C (the joystick in port 2 or the keyboard, set up from the options panel) and returns the movement as X (-1 left, 1 right) and Y (-1 up, 1 down), with the carry and fire_pressed set when fire is down; A holds the five bits, set for each direction pressed and bit 4 for fire.
The low byte of the call's target, rewritten to choose the control: $6F for read_keys at $516F, set by $7D0B, or $5E for read_joystick at $515E.
The high byte of the call's target ($51 for either reader); the code from here turns the five bits into X, Y and fire.
Reads the joystick in port 2: makes CIA 1's port A an input for the read, takes its five bits (active low) and puts the port back as an output.
The keyboard as a joystick: tests SPACE (fire), M (right), N (left), Z (down) and A (up) with key_down and packs them into five bits, low when pressed, the same as read_joystick.
The five key results read_keys builds, one rotated in after each test.
Turns on sprite X in $D015. Never called.
Turns off sprite X in $D015. Never called.
Four inline bytes: sprite number, x (two bytes) and y, given in the Spectrum's coordinates; adds the border offsets (27 and 50) and sets the sprite's position and its ninth x bit. Never called.
For make_sprite, by width in bytes (0 to 3): the step between bytes in the sprite's shape (0, 3, 2, 1).
For make_sprite, by width: the value the step is exclusive-ORed with after each byte; 3 for width 2, so the steps go 1, 2, 1, 2 and each row takes two bytes and skips the third.

Five inline bytes: sprite number, width in bytes (1 to 3), height in rows, colour, and shape number. Sets the sprite's colour, clears its 64 bytes at $DA00 + 64 × sprite (sprite_shapes_lo/hi) and copies the shape's rows from sprite_sources into it, one, two or three bytes a row.
The `sta` whose operand, one byte on, make_sprite rewrites; its own address is only the base the disassembler names.
The operand of `sta $527D,x` is the sprite's shape buffer, written by make_sprite before the copy; the code from here writes the bytes and steps to the next.
The high byte of the copy's destination.
The shape buffer of each of the eight sprites, $DA00 to $DBC0 in steps of 64, in bank 3, where pointers $68 to $6F at $DFF8 find them; this byte and the ones after it are low, high pairs.
The high bytes of the sprite buffers ($DA or $DB), read with the same index.

The four cursor shapes make_sprite copies, 16 rows of one byte each: $8E39 the arrow's outline, $8E49 its solid shape, drawn black behind it, $8E59 a second arrow with an outline inside the first, and $8E69 its solid shape (cursor_shapes).
The high bytes of sprite_sources, read with the same index ($5272).
Sixteen $FF bytes after the shape table that nothing reads.
The border colour halt_with_border keeps showing.
Never returns: shows border colour A until fire is pressed, again and again (border_until_fire). Its one caller is the script engine at $ADE1.
The colour border_until_fire shows.
Waits for fire to be let go, sets the border to colour A, waits for fire to be pressed and let go, and turns the border black again.
Steps the border colour on every frame until fire is pressed, then makes it black. Never called: a debugging aid.
Moves the bitmap pointer at $88/$89 down one pixel row: one byte on, or, from a cell's eighth row, to the first row of the cell below. One caller, $C2B9.
Puts the arrow cursor, sprites 0 and 1, at the position the current window keeps (its bytes 12, x, and 13, y; the window record is at $7E) and turns both sprites on.
Turns sprites 0 and 1, the cursor, on in $D015.
Turns sprites 0 and 1, the cursor, off in $D015.

Gives the cursor its second shape, the arrow with an outline inside (sprite_sources 2 and 3); from $5F14, its first, the plain arrow (0 and 1). Turns the cursor off and builds both sprites with make_sprite: sprite 0 white, one byte wide and 16 rows, over sprite 1 black, the solid shape behind it.
make_sprite's inline bytes for the cursor's white sprite: sprite 0, 1 byte wide, 16 rows, colour 1, and the shape number at $5F29, which cursor_shape2 rewrites (0 or 2).
make_sprite's inline bytes for the cursor's black sprite: sprite 1, 1 byte wide, 16 rows, colour 0, and the shape number at $5F31, rewritten to 1 or 3.
After building the two sprites, on into cursor_on.
Three inline bytes, x (two bytes) and y, copied to $A6-$A8, then the cursor is placed there as by cursor_place. Never called.

Places the cursor's two sprites at the position in $A6 (x, low), $A7 (x, high) and $A8 (y), in the 256 by 192 picture: adds 56 to x and 58 to y for the border and the picture's offset and sets both sprites' ninth x bit together.
A lone `rts` nothing reaches.

Five bytes for each open window: the save pointer ($28/$29) before it opened and the cursor's x (two bytes) and y, pushed by window_push and taken back by window_pop; 24 windows' room. At the hand-over it holds a fill pattern of $FF and $00 left in memory before the game was saved, overwritten as windows open.
The offset of the next free entry in window_stack.
Cleared at start-up and read by nothing else.
The eight inline bytes of the last window opened, copied here as they are into its record.

Opens a window. Eight inline bytes: column, row, width and height in cells of the area inside the frame (in the 32 by 24 picture), the colour byte for its cells, two more bytes kept in the record, and a flags byte whose bit 0 asks for a menu: the routine at $8545 draws it and the cursor is shown. Steps the window pointer $7E to the next 16-byte record and copies the bytes there, pushes the save pointer and the cursor's position (window_push), saves what the window and the frame one cell around it will cover (window_save), draws the frame (window_frame), colours the cells and sets the text position to x 2, row 0.

Closes the top window: takes back its position and size, puts the bitmap it covered back from the save area (window_restore), steps $7E back to the window below and pops the save pointer and the cursor's position (window_pop).
Takes the top window's position and clears its colour cells with fill_cells, with the value in X written into the code as the column. Never called; its five bytes after it are unused too.
Five bytes after unused_clear_window that nothing reads.
Copies the top window's first five bytes (column, row, width, height, colour) to $2C-$31 as close_window wants them.
Pushes the save pointer $28/$29 and the cursor's position $A6-$A8 onto window_stack.
Pops the cursor's position and the save pointer from window_stack, leaving the pointer in $07/$08 as well for window_restore.

Copies what the window and its frame will cover to the save area at $28/$29, which moves on past it: for each cell, row by row, its 8 bitmap bytes and then its colour byte. The save area starts at $2000, over the picture loaded there.
The operand of `lda $6141,y` is the address of the row's colour cells, set by window_save and moved 40 bytes a row.
The high byte of that address.
Copies one bitmap byte from ($2A),y to the save area and moves both on.
Copies one byte from the save area at ($07) back to the bitmap at ($2A),y.
The reverse of window_save: copies each cell's 8 bitmap bytes and colour byte back from the save area, starting at the pointer window_pop gave.
The operand of `sta $61B4,y` is the address of the row's colour cells, set by window_restore and moved 40 bytes a row.
The high byte of the colour cells' address for window_restore.
Draws the window's frame in the bitmap from the frame glyphs at $72B7: the top row (frame_top), the sides (frame_sides) and the bottom (frame_bottom).
The frame's top row: corner glyph 0, glyph 3 across and the corner glyph 6.
Each row between top and bottom: glyph 1 at the left, blank glyph 5 across, glyph 7 at the right.
The bottom row: corner glyph 2, glyph 4 across and corner glyph 8.
Draws glyph A across the window's width less its two corners.

The raster interrupt, once a frame on line $EB (irq_line): acknowledges it and sets the line again, plays the sound (sound_irq), saves the pointers at $80-$89, calls the routine whose address is at $6286 (irq_hook), restores them, counts down delay_count unless the two unused switches at $4E8E and $4E90 say not to, and returns with the I/O banked in or out as it found it.

The operand of `jsr $8DDA` here is the interrupt's hook: $8DDA (a lone `rts`) when nothing is moving, or a routine that animates something while the main code waits, written at $74F5, $7502, $79D4, $7CBE and $C771. The code from here restores the pointers and counts the delay.
The NMI handler: returns at once, so RESTORE does nothing.
A lone `rts` after the NMI handler that nothing reaches.

Sets up the machine: clears zero page (clear_zero_page), the video registers (video_init), the window stack (window_init), the sprites (sprites_init), white-on-light-blue colour cells everywhere (fill_screen_colour with $1E), stops the CIA interrupts (cias_off) and takes over the interrupt vectors (vectors_init).
Turns off every interrupt of both CIAs and clears what is pending.
Points the processor's own vectors at $FFFA and $FFFE at nmi and irq (the ROMs stay banked out), waits for the raster to be above line 256, and starts a raster interrupt on line $EB.
A lone `rts`, called once by hardware_init: a step left empty.
Puts the video chip in bank 3 ($C000-$FFFF) in bitmap mode with the screen (colour cells) at $DC00 and the bitmap at $E000, the border dark grey, 40 columns, no multicolour.
Fills all 1,000 colour cells at $DC00 with X, through fill with the colour written into its inline bytes.
fill's inline bytes: $03E8 bytes (1,000) of the value at $6378, rewritten with X, at $DC00.
Turns every sprite off, clears their positions, expansion, priority and multicolour bits, and sets the eight sprite pointers at $DFF8 to $68-$6F, the shapes at $DA00-$DBFF.
Empties the window stack and sets the save area to $2000.
Clears zero page from $02 to $FF.

Fills memory with a value. Five inline bytes: a count of bytes ($1F), a count of whole pages ($20), the value ($21) and the start address ($22/$23). Fills the whole pages first, then the odd bytes after them.
Five inline bytes, column, row, width, height and a value, as for fill_cells, but fills the bitmap bytes of the rectangle with the value, eight a cell. Never called.

Copies A bytes from after the call that called its caller into $1F onward, and makes that call return past them. It takes its own return address off the stack and writes it, plus one, into the `jmp` at $715C, takes the caller's return address, copies the bytes after it, pushes the address of the last of them back, and jumps back to its caller. Every routine that takes inline bytes starts `lda #n` / `jsr inline_args`.
The operand of this `jmp` is written by inline_args with the address it was called from plus one, so it goes back into its caller.
The low byte of the return jump's operand.
The high byte of the return jump's operand.
Copies inline bytes to the rectangle variables: $1F to $2C (column), $20 to $2E (row), $21 to $2F (width), $22 to $30 (height), $23 to $31 (value).
Banks the I/O chips in ($01 = $05: RAM with the I/O area at $D000).
Banks the I/O chips out ($01 = $04: RAM everywhere), the state the game keeps except while it touches a chip.
Five inline bytes, column, row, width, height and a colour: fills the rectangle's colour cells in screen memory, a row at a time. From $7186 it fills the rectangle already in $2C-$31.
Sets $2A/$2B and $88/$89 to the address in screen memory of column $2C, row $2E of the picture, from screen_rows.
The same as cell_address for column $84 and row $85.
The bitmap address of the pixel at x $2C/$2D, y $2E, as pixel_address does for an 8-bit x. Never called.

The bitmap address of the pixel at x $84, y $85 of the picture, in $2A/$2B and $88/$89: the cell's column times 8, plus the row within the cell, plus the row's address from bitmap_rows. Returns the pixel's position in its byte (x and 7) in A.

Two inline bytes, the address of a zero-terminated string, printed from the position at $67 and $69 with print_glyph; carriage returns move down a row and codes below 13 move the pointer by the offset at $09/$0A. Its glyphs would come from frame_glyphs, which holds only the nine frame pieces, so it would print nothing readable. Never called.
The operand of `lda $7247,x` is the string's address, written by unused_print.
Writes `rts` at $722B, so unused_print returns at once. Never called.
Writes `nop` back at $722B. Never called.
One character for unused_print: a carriage return moves down a row, a code from 13 up is printed as a glyph, a lower code moves the pointer by $09/$0A. Never called.
Copies glyph A of frame_glyphs, 8 bytes, into the bitmap at ($2A),Y; Y moves on 8, to the next cell. Used for the window frames.
`lda $72AB,x` with its operand written to the glyph's address; the code from here copies the 8 bytes.
The low byte of the glyph's address, written by print_glyph.
The high byte of the glyph's address.

Nine glyphs of 8 bytes for the window frames: 0 top-left corner, 1 left side, 2 bottom-left corner, 3 top edge, 4 bottom edge, 5 blank, 6 top-right corner, 7 right side, 8 bottom-right corner. The lines are one pixel thick, a pixel in from the cell's edge.
The bitmap address of the cell at column $2C, row $2E, in $2A/$2B and $88/$89.
The same for column $84 and row $85.
Moves the bitmap pointer $2A/$2B down one row of cells (320 bytes).
Moves the screen pointer on 80 bytes, two rows. Never called.
Moves the screen pointer $2A/$2B on 40 bytes, one row of colour cells.
Frames left to wait: set by wait_frames and counted down by the raster interrupt.
Waits A frames: sets delay_count and waits for the interrupt to count it to 0.
Takes two inline bytes and does nothing with them. Never called.
Two inline bytes, column and row, made into a bitmap address. Never called.
Six inline bytes, a rectangle and an address: copies the rectangle's bitmap bytes to that address. Never called.
Copies memory. Six inline bytes: the source address, the destination address, a count of bytes and a count of whole pages; the whole pages go first, then the odd bytes.
Adds A to the pointer at $2A/$2B.

A lone `rts`, called from 19 places: around the save and load (the four calls at $544F to $54A1, where the data is copied in memory instead), as a message window opens or a satellite moves, and at the end of a nuclear exchange. What the original did at those points is not known from this version.
Clears the radio's settings at $5E64-$5E67 and $5E69 and sets $5E6A to 8 and $5E6B to 7. One caller, new_game.
Fills the five-byte entry buffer at $740E with spaces (fill) and empties it ($5E69 = 0).
fill's inline bytes: 5 bytes, no pages, of $20 (space), at $740E.
Counts one more character in the entry buffer, clearing it when five are already there. Never called.
Two zero bytes nothing reads.
The five characters typed on the radio's keypad, then '$' to end them as a string, and a zero.
Moves the radio's frequency ($5E6A/$5E6B) up one kHz, from the band's top ($5E6D/$5E6E) round to its bottom ($5E6F/$5E70).
Moves the frequency down one kHz, from the band's bottom round to its top.

Shows the frequency on the radio's display: makes it five decimal digits in entry_buffer (number_to_digits) and draws them with the big digits (radio_draw_entry), keeping the count of typed digits as it was.
Counted up by the interrupt hooks radio_scan_irq and unscramble_irq, which act on one frame in four and one in two.
The interrupt hook while the radio scans: on every fourth frame moves the frequency up one (radio_freq_up) and redraws it, saving and restoring the pointers the drawing uses.
Makes radio_scan_irq the interrupt's hook, so the frequency climbs on its own.
Sets the interrupt's hook back to the lone `rts` at $8DDA, stopping a scan or the unscrambling.

The radio, from the main screen: clears the entry, opens a window at column 1, row 1, 16 by 2, draws the radio's picture (picture 0) over it and shows the frequency, restarting the scan if it was on. Then, until fire is pressed off the panel, waits for fire (radio_wait_fire) and handles the button under the cursor (radio_button). Leaves with the scan stopped.
open_window's inline bytes for the radio: column 1, row 1, 16 by 2 cells, colour $02, flags 0.

Finds what the cursor is on from the colour cell under it: only a cell coloured $61 is a button. Six or more cells from the panel's left edge it is the keypad (radio_keypad); otherwise the cursor's row in the window (record byte 11) picks the button in the left-hand column: above row 8 SCAN START/STOP, which turns the scan on or off ($5E67) and flashes the button; rows 8 and 9 the up arrow (radio_up); row 10 BAND (radio_band); below it the down arrow (radio_down).
Flashes a rectangle of colour cells eight times, two frames each, by flipping their two low bits: the button's response to a press. From $7812 the size is in $84 and $85.
Calls fill_cells_86 and returns; nothing calls it.
Fills a rectangle of colour cells ($84 wide, $85 high, at $88/$89) with the value made from the first cell's low nibble and $86's (combine_nibbles).
BAND: stops the scan, moves to the next of the six bands (0 to 5, $5E65), sets its limits (radio_set_band) and puts the frequency at the band's bottom.
Sets the band's bottom ($5E6F/$5E70) and top ($5E6D/$5E6E) from band_bottoms and band_tops, and stops the scan.
Two zero bytes before band_bottoms that nothing reads.
The bottom frequency of each band in kHz: 1800, 3500, 7000, 14000, 21000 and 28500.
1799, the frequency just below band 0: radio_find_band compares with it first, then with band_tops.
The high byte of 1799, read by radio_find_band at its first step.
The top frequency of each band in kHz: 3499, 6999, 13999, 20999, 25000 and 50000. Between 25000 and 28500 is no band.

After a frequency is typed: finds its band (radio_find_band). Below 1800 it becomes 1800, in band 0; from 25000 to 28499, the gap between bands 4 and 5, it becomes 28500, in band 5. Then it sets the band's limits and shows the frequency.
Counts in $5E6C how many of 1799 and the six band tops the frequency reaches, one more than the number of its band. At 50000 or more it sets the frequency to 49999.

EXECUTE on the keypad: stops the scan, flashes the key, reads the typed digits as a number (parse_number) and makes it the frequency (radio_tune_typed); the entry then counts as full, so the next digit starts a new one.
The up arrow: stops the scan, moves the frequency up one and flashes the arrow.
The down arrow: stops the scan, moves the frequency down one and flashes the arrow.
Goes to radio_execute.

A press on the keypad: row 12 of the window is EXECUTE (radio_execute); otherwise the key is worked out from the cursor's row and column, 1 to 9 in three rows of three, then 0 (counted as 10), AM (11) and FM (12) along the bottom row. Flashes it (keypad_flash) and adds it to the entry (keypad_digit).
Waits for fire to be let go (wait_fire_up).
Flashes the key in $5E68 (2 cells by 1) at its place in the panel, from keypad_positions.
flash_cells for a rectangle of $84 by $85 cells at $88/$89.

Where each key sits in the radio's window, column and row, for keypad_flash: 0 at (6, 10); 1 to 9 at columns 6, 9 and 12 of rows 4, 6 and 8; an entry for 10 that is never used, since key 10 becomes 0 first; AM at (9, 10) and FM at (12, 10).
Waits for fire to be let go, then moves the cursor once a frame until fire is pressed.
Returns: the AM key (11) adds nothing to the entry.
Returns: the FM key (12) adds nothing either. AM and FM only flash.
A digit key (0 to 9): if five digits were already typed it clears the entry first, then adds the digit to entry_buffer and redraws it. AM and FM add nothing.
Fills the entry with spaces, draws them (radio_draw_entry) and sets the count of typed digits to 0.
Draws the typed digits in entry_buffer in the radio's display, one big digit a cell, from the cell below and right of the panel's corner.
Draws one character of the display: a space blank (the 16 zero bytes at $794B), a digit from big_digits, two cells tall, 8 bytes each.
The operand of `lda $792E,x` is the glyph's address, written by draw_big_digit; the code from here copies its 16 bytes into two cells.
The low byte of the glyph's address.
The high byte of the big digit's address.
Sixteen zero bytes, the space in the radio's display.

Shows an intercepted message to unscramble. Expands the text at $88 into the buffer at $AC25 (expand_text), opens a window with the filter panel (picture 5) and a window for the message inside it, and takes the scramble key for the country sending ($8A), or the key for nothing when the scan is off, from scramble_keys. Starts the unscrambling hook (unscramble_irq) and lets the player click the eight filters f0 to f7: each click flips one bit of the filter setting. Fire outside the panel closes both windows.
open_window's inline bytes for the filter panel: column 1, row 16, 28 by 4 cells, colour $1A.
open_window's inline bytes for the message: column 6, row 2, 20 by 7 cells, colour $57.
A lone `rts` after radio_keypad's last routine that nothing reaches.
Turns the cursor off, makes the message window current again, marks the text as finished ($7BA0 = 25) so the hook stops, and closes both windows.
The eight filter buttons, six bytes each in the form hit_test reads: column, row, width, height and two zero bytes; 3 cells apart along the panel's bottom row.
The interrupt hook while a message is shown: on every second frame prints the message's next character in its window, through scramble_char, until the text ends; then marks it finished.

Garbles a character according to how near the filters are to the key: counts the bits in which the setting ($7B9F) matches the key ($7B9D). With all eight matching it returns the character as it is; otherwise it returns it when a random number is below 32 times the matches, and a random character from $20 to $3F when not. Each filter set right lets another eighth of the message through.
The message window's record address, kept while the filter panel is the current window.
The high byte of the message window's address.
The address of the expanded message, the start the hook goes back to.
The high byte of the message's address.
The hook's place in the message.
The high byte of the hook's place.
The key of the message being shown, from scramble_keys.
The number of the filter just clicked, 0 to 7.
The eight filters, a bit each, flipped as they are clicked.
25 when the message is finished or closed; until then the hook goes on.
The bit each filter flips: f0 $01 to f7 $80, and a zero after them.
The last number random gave.
The random generator's three bytes of state, here and at $7BAC and $7BAD; random_init seeds them.
The random generator's second byte of state.
The random generator's third byte of state, seeded from the raster line.

Returns a pseudo-random byte in A (and in $04 and random_out): rotates the first state byte right by three, adds the other two, rotates the sum left by two and shifts the state along, keeping $0D and $0E as it found them. The game's decisions and the scrambled characters all come from it.
Seeds the random generator: 0, $AD, $CE and twice the raster line the beam is on, so each game differs.
Is country $8A on the band the radio is tuned to? Compares its band in country_bands with the radio's band ($5E65); returns with Z set when they are the same.

The radio band each country transmits in, 0 to 5, in the order of the country list: Canada 0, U.S.A 0, Central American Alliance 0, European Unite 1, Libya 2, Argentina 3, Black African Republic 1, South Africa 1, Israel 4, Islamic Alliance 5, Pakistan 1, India 0, Australia 2, China 2, Japan 5, Eastern Block 1.
The filter setting that unscrambles each country's messages, one byte a country in the same order ($9C for Canada to $54 for the Eastern Block), and a 17th, $00, used when the radio is not scanning.

The game proper: resets the stack, sets up the machine (hardware_init), colours the picture area (fill_cells), clears the eight window records at $8C67 and makes the first a whole-screen window, then shows the options panel (options_panel). From $7CBB, where the game also comes back after a RAMLOAD, a quit or a message that ends a turn: sets the interrupt hook to nothing, gives the cursor its arrow, starts a new game (new_game) and the week's first report ($BAA1), and goes into the main loop.
fill_cells' inline bytes: the 32 by 24 picture from column 0, row 1, with colour $15, white on green.

The main loop, once a frame: moves the game clock on (game_clock), waits a frame, moves the cursor with the controls (move_cursor) and, when fire is pressed on one of the six icons of main_icons (hit_test), goes to its routine through icon_routines with this loop as the return (on_goto).
A lone `rts` after the main loop's dispatch that nothing reaches.

Sets the keyboard as the control, starts tune 0, the only music, and opens the options panel: a window with picture 10 and the keys, "F1 KEYBOARD OPTION" and "F3 JOYSTICK #2". Waits for F1 or F3; F3 makes read_controls use the joystick.
open_window's inline bytes for the options panel: column 5, row 8, 14 by 10 cells, colour $10.
The options panel's text, after `jsr print_inline`: "A=up,Z=down", "n=left,m=right", "space=fire", "F1 KEYBOARD OPTION", "F3 JOYSTICK #2", ended by '$'.
Tests F1 (matrix $04) and F3 ($05) until one is down; F1 leaves the keyboard, F3 sets read_controls to read_joystick. Closes the panel.
The early return of game_clock.

The game's clock, called once each time round the main loop: counts $5B54 to 192, then moves the hour count $5B55 on one and runs the timed events: every hour the countries' moves (country_events); in every four hours, the radio intercept in the first (radio_intercept) and the Big Bird report in the second (bigbird_report); every eight hours the end-of-week report ($BAA1).
Raises every one of the 256 bytes of the relationship table at $5C5C by one, stopping at $FF. One caller, $BAE6.
Raises the 16 bytes of country $8A's row of the relationship table by one, stopping at $FF.
Goes to the routine the table at $07/$08 names for the number in $04 (1 for the first word), with the address in $88/$89 pushed as its return, so the routine's `rts` goes there.
The `jmp` whose operand on_goto writes with the chosen routine.
The low byte of on_goto's jump.
The high byte of on_goto's jump.
The radio icon: turns the cursor off, runs the radio (radio_panel) and shows the cursor again.

Is the cursor in one of X rectangles of six bytes at $80 (column, row, width, height in cells, and two bytes where the cursor's position is left)? Returns with the carry set and the number counted down from X, so the last rectangle is 1, or the carry clear when it is in none.
Is the cursor (the current window's bytes 12 and 13) inside the rectangle at $80? Writes the cursor's x and y into the rectangle's bytes 4 and 5 and returns with the carry set when it is inside.
The routines of the six icons, last first: the radio ($7E63), the OUT tray ($81FC), the IN tray ($824D), U.N.N. Force ($829D), Information ($7F0C) and the satellites ($C2E4).

The six icons of the main screen as hit_test rectangles: the satellites (column 2, row 3, 6 by 5), Information (2, 10), U.N.N. Force (2, 17), the IN tray (10, 17, 7 by 3), the OUT tray (10, 20, 7 by 3) and the radio (18, 17, 7 by 6).

The Information icon: opens a window and draws four pictures in it (1 to 4), then waits for fire on one of them (info_choices) and goes to its report through info_routines, with the main loop as the return.
open_window's inline bytes for the Information choice: column 1, row 7, 8 by 8 cells, colour $30.
A lone `rts` after icon_information that nothing reaches.
The four pictures of the Information window as hit_test rectangles: (1, 7), (5, 7), (1, 11) and (5, 11), each 2 or 3 cells wide.
The Information window's four routines, last rectangle first: close and return ($7F9C), missile power ($7FF0), technology ($7FFC) and natural resources ($8008).
The Information window's own picture: drops on_goto's return, closes the window and goes back with the cursor shown and its first shape.
Which countries a report marks in colour: 0 none, 1 country A ($8A), 2 country B ($8B), 3 both. Set only while the script commands $3F to $47 show a report.
Script commands $45, $46 and $47 (from $7FAE, $7FBC and $7FC0): the missile report with country A, B or both marked.
Script commands $3F, $40 and $41: the technology report with country A, B or both marked.
Script commands $42, $43 and $44: the natural resources report with country A, B or both marked.
The missile report: "Missile Power (Estimates)" with MX1, MX2 and MX3 for each country (bytes 6, 7 and 8 of its record).
The technology report: "Technology Capability" as a percentage for each country (byte 5 of its record, followed by a 0).
The natural resources report: "Natural Resources" as a percentage (byte 4 of its record, followed by a 0).

Shows a report: turns the cursor off, opens a window 28 by 17 at (1, 1), prints the heading and the country list, then each country's figures in columns (report_missiles_rows or report_percent_rows), marks the countries report_marks asks for, and waits for fire before closing.
open_window's inline bytes for a report: column 1, row 1, 28 by 17 cells, colour $15.
For each of the 16 countries, MX1, MX2 and MX3 printed at x 144, 176 and 200 on the country's row.
Marks the countries asked for, waits for a press of fire, closes the report and shows the cursor.
Marks country A's row, B's row or both, by report_marks.
Colours country A's row of the report $57 (light green on yellow).
Colours country B's row of the report $67.
The screen address of country A's row in the report window, and its width less one in Y.
For each country, one byte of its record printed at x 144 with a 0 after it: byte 5 (technology), or byte 4 from $8179 (natural resources).
The operand of `ldy #$05` is the record byte the percentage report prints, 5 or 4.
Sets the byte printed to 4 and goes on as report_tech_rows.

The three reports' headings, each ended by a carriage return and '$': " Missile Power (Estimates)   MX1    MX2  MX3", " Natural Resources        Percentage" and " Technology Capability     Percentage".
The OUT tray: opens a window listing the eight standard letters (menu 6), waits for a choice (menu_choice) and goes to the letter's routine through letter_routines; all eight are write_letter.
open_window's inline bytes for the letter list: column 5, row 5, 20 by 8 cells, colour $16, flags 7, a menu (list 6).
The `rts` on_goto returns through after a letter.
The routines of the eight letters, all write_letter ($84B9).
Waits for fire, then takes the row of the menu the cursor was on (window byte 11) as the choice in letter_choice, closes the window and returns the choice plus one.
The letter or menu item last chosen, 0 for the first.
The IN tray: turns the cursor off and shows the oldest letter waiting (in_tray_next), or "No Mail in Mail Box." when there is none.
Shows "No Mail in Mail Box." in a small window until fire is pressed.
open_window's inline bytes for the empty IN tray: column 5, row 17, 15 by 1 cells, colour $B7.
The text "No Mail in Mail Box.", ended by '$', after `jsr print_inline`.
Calls wait_fire_or_time; nothing reaches it.
Waits 20 frames or until fire is pressed, whichever comes first.
The U.N.N. Force icon: turns the cursor off, runs force_menu and shows the cursor.

Where the force is, and where to send it. When it is stationed ($5B57 = 0) the force's report runs first (force_report, event script $21) and Exit ends there. Re-direct opens the country list (choose_country): a country that is gone, or the one the force is in or going to, is refused (force_refused). Otherwise the country becomes the target ($5B56) and $5B57, the weeks until it arrives, goes up by one, to 3 at most. Then script $20 tells of the move with its own Exit and Re-direct, and the choice repeats while Re-direct is chosen.
Runs event script $21 with the force's country as the name in the text: "U.N.N Forces are in ..." with Exit and Re-direct.

Says why the force cannot go: "Cannot go there." for a country that is gone, "Forces are allready there." (the original's spelling) for the one it is in, or "Forces are going there." when it is already on its way.
open_window's inline bytes for the force's reply: column 5, row 20, 20 by 1 cells, colour $61.
The text "Forces are allready there.", ended by '$'.
Waits for fire or 20 frames and closes the window.
The text "Cannot go there.", ended by '$'.
The text "Forces are going there.", ended by '$', followed by a `jmp force_refused_end`.

Text pieces for the force's scripts: "U.N.N Forces are"; at $83CC "... in" with the country's name ('@' pieces, below); at $83DB "TROOP MOVEMENT"; at $83EC "... to arrive in" the country "within" the number of weeks in $5B57 "week(s)."; each piece ended by '$'.
The force's report: "TROOP MOVEMENT", "U.N.N Forces are", "in" and the country at $5B34, built from '@' references to the pieces around it.
"TROOP MOVEMENT" between carriage returns, ended by '$'.
The force's move: "TROOP MOVEMENT", "U.N.N Forces are", "to arrive in" the country at $5B34, "within" the number at $5B57 "week(s).".
Waits 200 frames. Nothing calls it.
Moves the cursor once a frame (move_cursor) until fire is pressed.
Waits for fire to be let go and then pressed.
Waits until fire is not pressed.
Opens the country list (a menu, list 0) and returns the country chosen, 0 to 15, in A and country_chosen, and its name's address in country_chosen_name.
open_window's inline bytes for the country list: column 1, row 1, 16 by 17 cells, colour $6F, flags 1, a menu (list 0).
The country chosen in choose_country.
A byte after country_chosen that nothing reads.
The address of the chosen country's name, from country_names.
The high byte of the name's address.
A byte before letter_window that nothing reads.
Opens the window letters and memos are shown in, 17 by 15 at (13, 2), and draws the envelope picture (picture 7) at its top, with the text starting on its fifth row.
open_window's inline bytes for a letter: column 13, row 2, 17 by 15 cells, colour $16.

Writes the letter chosen in the OUT tray: shows its text from letter_texts (where '*' asks for the country it goes to), then the Send letter and Exit menu. On Send letter it shows "Letter sent." and runs the letter's script from letter_scripts, which carries out what the letter asks of the countries chosen.
open_window's inline bytes for "Letter sent.": column 3, row 20, 7 by 1 cells, colour $63.
The text "Letter sent.", ended by '$'.
Shows the Send letter and Exit menu (list 14) and returns the row chosen: 0 Send letter, 1 Exit.
open_window's inline bytes for the Send letter menu: column 3, row 19, 10 by 2 cells, colour $63, flags 15, a menu (list 14).
Prints a window's menu: its flags byte, less bit 0, picks the list from menu_lists, printed one item a line.

The menus' item lists, by a window's flags less bit 0: 0 the country list ($5340), 2 "Ignore, Yes, No", 4 "Exit, Re-direct", 6 the eight letters, 8 "Neutral, Support, Criticise, Ask for Talks", 10 "Ignore, Agree, Criticise", 12 the options panel's two lines ($7D85), 14 "Send letter, Exit", 16 "Ignore, Agree, Disagree", 18 "View Data, Agree, Disagree", 20 "CARRY ON, RAMSAVE GAME, RAMLOAD GAME, QUIT GAME".
The menus' items, each ended by '$' and each list by a second '$': the lists named in menu_lists, from "Ignore" to "QUIT GAME".
